case_studies.title: Honeyval: A Comprehensive Evaluation Framework for LLM-powered HTTP Honeypots
case_studies.abstract: Honeypots are decoy systems mimicking real system components designed to defend against cyber attacks. Recently, LLMs increasingly serve as simulation backbones for honeypots. They enable defenders to construct high-interaction honeypots with low system security risks. However, LLM-powered honeypot development lacks a unified evaluation framework. Most evaluations consist of measuring response similarity on fixed commands, manual testing, or real-world deployment. These methods are often not scalable for development, reproducible across evaluations, representative of practical attacks, or adap
case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of evaluating LLM-powered honeypots by building a comprehensive evaluation framework called Honeyval, which resulted in a more efficient and scalable way to test these decoy systems. The framework helps to defend against cyber attacks by mimicking real system components. The research is relevant to IT infrastructure work as it improves honeypot development.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage cloud-based security infrastructure, here is what to do: review your current honeypot setup, consider integrating LLM-powered honeypots, and evaluate them using the Honeyval framework to improve your defence against cyber attacks. This flags a risk: if your org uses traditional honeypots, check their effectiveness immediately and consider upgrading to LLM-powered ones.
case_studies.score_reasoning: Paper presents a new framework for evaluating LLM-powered honeypots, which is relevant to IT security and deployment of LLMs. It could be used to build or evaluate LLM-based security services, but the specific actionability is limited to IT security professionals.

case_studies.title: LLMSurgeon: Diagnosing Data Mixture of Large Language Models
case_studies.abstract: The pretraining data mixture of Large Language Models (LLMs) constitutes their "digital DNA", shaping model behaviors, capabilities, and failure modes. Yet this composition is rarely disclosed, making post-hoc auditing of data combination or provenance difficult. In this work, we formalize $\textbf{Data Mixture Surgery (DMS)}$: given only generated text from a target LLM, estimate the domain-level distribution of its pretraining corpus under a predefined taxonomy. We propose $\textbf{LLMSurgeon}$, a strong framework that casts DMS as an inverse problem under the label-shift assumption. Rather
case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of identifying the pretraining data mixture of Large Language Models, by building a framework called LLMSurgeon that can estimate the domain-level distribution of the pretraining corpus. The result is a tool that can diagnose the 'digital DNA' of these models, making it easier to audit their data combination or provenance. This research may have implications for those using LLMs in their IT infrastructure, particularly in terms of understanding and mitigating potential biases or errors.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage LLM-based systems, here is what to do: review your model's documentation to see if the pretraining data mixture is disclosed, check if your organisation has any auditing or testing procedures in place for LLMs, and consider using a tool like LLMSurgeon to estimate the domain-level distribution of the pretraining corpus. This flags a risk: if your org uses LLMs without understanding their pretraining data mixture, check for potential biases or errors immediately. Not directly applicable to general cloud infrastructure work, but relevant to those working with LLMs.

case_studies.title: Do Proactive Agents Really Need an LLM to Decide When to Wake and What to Anchor?
case_studies.abstract: Proactive agents read user activity as text and call an LLM on every event to decide whether to act. But user activity is not natively text: it is a structured event stream of (actor, verb, object, timestamp) tuples that the operating system already maintains in graph form. Rendering the structure as text and asking an LLM to recover it is a round-trip the system never had to take. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of proactive agents relying on large language models to decide when to act, by building a small temporal-graph-learning model that treats user activity as graph updates rather than text. The result is a more efficient approach to proactive agent decision-making. This research is not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work.

High IT_RELEVANCE due to agentic systems and potential automation benefits. case_studies.title: EASE Configuration Facilitates A Reproducible Science of LLM Social Simulations
case_studies.abstract: LLMs are increasingly deployed to simulate social interactions, yet many of the existing simulators remain ad hoc and monolithic. This lack of architectural standardization prevents reproducible research and complicates downstream evaluation. We advance a rigorous science of LLM-based multi-agent simulation by modularizing core components into Environments, Agents, Simulation engines, and Evaluation metrics (EASE). We demonstrate the utility of EASE configuration by wrapping it in an experimental study schema for orchestrating workflows centered around answering explicit research questions in
case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of non-reproducible science in Large Language Model (LLM) social simulations by creating a modular framework called EASE. The EASE configuration allows for standardized and reproducible research. The result is a more rigorous science of LLM-based multi-agent simulation.
case_studies.it_breakdown: Not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work, as it focuses on a modular framework for LLM social simulations, which is more relevant to research and development rather than cloud infrastructure management.

case_studies.title: First head-to-head comparison of agentic AI applied to the analysis of simulated data of the Einstein Telescope
case_studies.abstract: We report a comparison of two state-of-the-art agentic AI systems, Claude Code (Anthropic) and Codex (OpenAI), tasked with autonomously executing a simple end-to-end gravitational wave data analysis pipeline on a shared computing infrastructure without human intervention. The pipeline comprises power spectral density estimation from raw Einstein Telescope simulated noise, geometric template bank generation, matched filter recovery of 100 binary black hole signal injections, automated results generation, and large language model-assisted production of a manuscript formatted in the style of Phys
case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of automating gravitational wave data analysis by building and comparing two agentic AI systems, achieving autonomous execution of a data analysis pipeline without human intervention. The result shows the potential of AI in scientific data analysis. This research is not directly relevant to IT infrastructure work.

case_studies.title: GenClaw: Code-Driven Agentic Image Generation
case_studies.abstract: Image generation models have evolved from text-conditioned pixel synthesis toward multimodal agents endowed with visual comprehension and tool invocation capabilities. Yet, existing agents remain at the mercy of underlying black-box image models. Their workflow is trapped in a repetitive cycle of prompt rewriting for generation refinement, leaving them with no mechanism to directly manipulate the canvas. In essence, the potential of LLMs to serve as a genuine "brush" for precise visual construction remains largely untapped. In this paper, we propose GenClaw, a code-driven agentic image generat
case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of limited control in image generation models by introducing GenClaw, a code-driven agentic image generation model that allows for more precise visual construction. The authors built GenClaw to address the limitations of existing agents that rely on black-box image models. The result is a more direct and refined image generation process.
